title: Make Lexicographically Smallest Array by Swapping Elements
pattern: Sorting + Connected Components via Consecutive Gaps
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<pair<int,int>> sortedNums: n entries → O(n)
- vector<int> values (temporary, worst case one group): up to n entries → O(n)
- vector<int> indices (temporary, worst case one group): up to n entries → O(n)
- sort() stack: O(log n)
- not counted: input nums, returned result
approach: Two elements can be swapped if their value difference is ≤ limit. By transitivity, any chain of swappable values forms a connected component whose members can be freely rearranged among their original positions. After sorting the array by value, these components become contiguous runs separated by gaps > limit. For each run, we collect the values (already sorted) and their original indices, sort the indices, and assign the smallest value to the smallest index - yielding the lexicographically smallest result.
hints: If value a can swap with b, and b can swap with c, what does that tell you about where a, b, and c can ultimately be placed relative to each other? The constraint n ≤ 10^5 rules out checking every pair of indices directly.

Sort the (value, original index) pairs, then split into contiguous groups where consecutive sorted values differ by at most `limit`. For nums = [1,5,3,9,8] with limit 2, sorted values [1,3,5,8,9] give groups {1,3,5} and {8,9}.

```
sort (value, index) pairs by value
i = 0
while i < n:
    j = i
    while j < n and (j == i or sorted[j].val - sorted[j-1].val <= limit):
        collect sorted[j].val and sorted[j].index
        j++
    sort collected indices
    assign collected values (already ascending) to sorted indices
    i = j
return result
```

**Gap equals limit exactly** - adjacent sorted values differ by exactly `limit`, so they belong to the same group.
`Input: nums = [1,5,3,9,8], limit = 2` → `Expected: [1,3,5,8,9]`
⚠️ Bug: using `<` instead of `<=` in the gap check → returns `[1,5,3,8,9]`

**Single element** - n = 1, no swaps are possible.
`Input: nums = [5], limit = 1` → `Expected: [5]`
⚠️ Bug: returning an empty vector when the loop body is skipped → returns `[]`

**No valid swaps** - every consecutive gap in the sorted array exceeds `limit`.
`Input: nums = [1,7,28,19,10], limit = 3` → `Expected: [1,7,28,19,10]`
⚠️ Bug: ignoring the gap condition and treating all elements as one group → returns `[1,7,10,19,28]`

**Unsorted indices within a group** - indices must be sorted so the smallest value lands at the smallest position.
`Input: nums = [1,7,6,18,2,1], limit = 3` → `Expected: [1,6,7,18,1,2]`
⚠️ Bug: assigning values to indices in collection order without sorting indices → returns `[1,7,6,18,2,1]`

followUps.q: What if you must also minimize the total number of swaps used?
followUps.a: Within each group, the minimum swaps to reach the target permutation equals (group size − number of cycles) in the index mapping. Trace each cycle by following original index → sorted position. TC stays O(n log n), SC stays O(n).

followUps.q: What if the array is too large to fit in memory and arrives as a stream?
followUps.a: Use external merge sort on (value, index) pairs, then scan the sorted stream to identify groups by gaps and build the result. The grouping logic is identical but operates on a buffered stream. TC: O(n log n), SC: O(B) where B is the chunk/buffer size.

followUps.q: What if the swap condition is "nums[i] and nums[j] share a common divisor greater than 1" instead of a value difference?
followUps.a: Transitivity still holds through shared factors. Use DSU where each value is unioned with all its prime factors. Two values in the same factor-component can be freely rearranged. TC: O(n · √max_val · α(n)), SC: O(n + max_val).
